newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: New Congo government to regulate money changers.
newsitem.headline: New Congo government to regulate money changers.

text.p: Money changers on the informal "Wall Street" market in downtown Kinshasa, capital of Laurent Kabila's newly named Democratic Republic of Congo, on Saturday poured cold water on a government bid to regulate their trade.
State radio announced on Thursday that Finance Minister Mawapanga Mwana Nanga, intended to control the chaotic money market by charging each trader $50 to register for a licence.
Those who did not pay would be outlawed, the radio said, without specifying what penalty awaited offenders.

"Will they succeed? I don't think so," said Beatrice, holding a thick wad of the country's traditionally unstable currency, still known as the "zaire" despite the change in the Central African country's name.

"There are three factors in this profession -- chance, courage and contacts. Chance is what the good Lord gives. Courage enables me to grab trade off another trader and contacts is knowing people who bring you business," Beatrice added.
"Paying $50 for a licence does not come into it."
Other moneychangers on "Wall Street" agreed the move would be difficult to implement.
Since coming to power last month after ousting long-term dictator Mobutu Sese Seko in a seven-month military campaign, Kabila's administration has met with some success in curbing rampant inflation.
However, attempts by the new authorities to stabilise the exchange rate by fixing it on a weekly basis have been met with scorn from the hundreds of money changers who animate central Kinshasa.
They say the official rate is rarely followed for more than a day.
Last weekend, students went on a rampage after the zaire slumped to around 160,000 to the dollar. The rate fell back to 120,000 before stabilising at around 140,000 by the end of the week.
The latest government fixing on Friday set the rate at 135,000 -- the same as the previous week.
Under Mobutu's corrupt rule, changing money was one of the few means to earn a daily living for many of the city's unemployed, estimated at as much as 70 percent of the population.
Financial business was conducted largely in the informal sector after the population lost confidence in the banks.

"The bad money chases the good. When there is a flood of zaires on the market and a scarcity of hard currency, the rate rises. If the rate is fixed it's hard to make a living," said Destiny, a student who swapped an education for the money trade when her family could no longer afford tuition fees.
The government has announced its intention at a later stage to replace the zaire currency, still stamped with Mobutu's image, with the Congolese franc.
Finance Minister Mawampanga Mwana Nanga has said the government will make the change without warning -- to avoid speculation.
Until then, money changers say the zaire currency is likely to continue on its meandering course.
